newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African crime "stabilises" in 1996, but rapes up.
newsitem.headline: S.African crime "stabilises" in 1996, but rapes up.

text.p: Reported rapes in South Africa, already the highest rate in the world, increased again in 1996, but police figures showed that other violent crimes declined slightly.

Murders, "carjackings" and drug-related crime, news of which has helped scare off tourists and foreign investors, decreased from 1995 but with violent crime still at relatively high levels, few South Africans will be sighing with relief yet.

"Crime levels in South Africa remain unacceptably high," Sydney Mufamadi, police minister, told a news conference, but said he was pleased that the situation, with 1.8 million crimes reported last year, seemed to be stabilising.
Murders fell to 61.1 per 100,000 people in 1996 from 64.6 the year before. Burglaries stayed level but serious assault and illegal possession of firearms crept up.
Mufamadi said the typical murder victim in South Africa was killed with a knife or a broken bottle by an acquaintance with whom he had got into a drunken weekend brawl.

Reported rapes nationwide rose last year to 119.5 per 100,000 people, out of a population estimated at 42 million, from 115.2 in 1995 and 105.3 in 1994, though police think they are told about at most one in 20 rapes.
Interpol put South Africa at the top of the rape table for its 89 members in 1994, with a reported incidence three times that of the United States and 12 times Germany's.
In financially motivated crime, the industrial province of Gauteng is the worst place in South Africa, and most of its crime is concentrated in the "crime capital" Johannesburg.
Gauteng's rates for burglary, robbery, vehicle theft and carjacking -- when drivers are forced to hand over cars, usually at gunpoint -- are up to three times the average.

Many South Africans from other regions shudder at the thought of even visiting Johannesburg, the brash city where anyone who can afford it puts bars, towering walls and electric fences round their homes and employs armed security services.

Last year, one in 1,000 cars was hijacked in Gauteng, though police said this showed a drop of more than 18 percent from 1995. A total of 5,789 of the province's seven million residents were murdered, slightly fewer than the year before.

Polls show crime is nightmare number one for South Africans. The country suffers from a culture of violence, guns, brutality and disrespect for human life that evolved during apartheid and the armed struggle against it, sociologists say.

President Nelson Mandela's three-year-old government, South Africa's first democratic authority, has announced numerous anti-crime plans and Mufamadi said the statistics, which improved markedly in late 1996, show they are finally working.
But ordinary people, each with a personal crime tale to tell, remain cynical.
They take a wry delight in ironic reports such as the theft of a bank cash machine, from police headquarters in Pretoria, or a burglary at minister Mufamadi's home by a corrupt policeman.
The clear-up rate of crimes fell to less than half in 1996, and the number of unsolved open cases continued to pile up, with 618,000 carried over to 1997 -- 47 for each detective.

The government, though not brushing aside the gravity of the problem, points out that blacks lived for decades with similarly high crime rates but few police to turn to, without the media outcry that has come now whites are affected too.
